description:
The Astronaut Health Informatics & Telemetry Engine (AHITE) is an integrated, real-time medical monitoring and diagnostic software designed for crewed spaceflights, lunar habitats, and interplanetary missions (such as Mars transit).

Because deep space missions experience significant communication latency (up to 20+ minutes one-way to Mars), the software must be heavily decentralized. It operates primarily as an on-board edge-computing platform with autonomous triage and diagnostic AI.
summary:
**ASTERA – Human Space Physiology Simulator**

ASTERA is an interactive educational platform developed to explore how different space environments affect the human body and human survival beyond Earth. It allows users to explore worlds such as the Moon, Mars, Venus, Jupiter, the ISS and deep space, understanding environmental factors like gravity, atmospheric pressure, temperature and radiation.

The project includes an interactive 3D Human Body Simulator that explains how space conditions may affect organs and body systems. It also features body comparisons, space activity simulations, a survival center and a mission simulator that illustrates potential health changes during long-duration missions.

ASTERA addresses the challenge by making complex space physiology concepts easier to explore and understand through interactive 3D visuals, comparisons and educational information. It highlights important risks such as bone and muscle loss, radiation exposure, fluid shifts and psychological stress, along with possible protective measures.

This project is important because understanding how space affects human health is essential for safer future space exploration. ASTERA aims to inspire students and space enthusiasts while helping them understand the challenges of protecting human life beyond Earth.

*Note: The simulator is for educational purposes and uses simplified models and illustrative estimates, not actual astronaut measurements or medical predictions.*
details:
Project Details – ASTERA: Human Space Physiology Simulator

What does the project do and how does it work?

ASTERA is an interactive 3D web-based simulator designed to demonstrate how different space environments affect the human body. Users can explore Earth, the International Space Station (ISS), the Moon, Mars, Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, Saturn, Europa, Titan and deep space.

The website works through several interactive modules:

  • Explore Worlds: Displays environmental conditions such as gravity, atmospheric pressure, temperature, radiation and potential hazards.
  • 3D Human Body Simulator: Allows users to select organs and body systems, including the brain, heart, lungs, bones, muscles, eyes and kidneys, to understand how space conditions may affect them.
  • Body Comparison: Compares health-related indicators across Earth, the ISS, the Moon, Mars and deep space.
  • Space Activities: Simulates activities such as sleeping, exercising, walking on the Moon or Mars, and performing spacewalks.
  • Survival Center: Explains the spacesuits, habitats, life-support systems and technologies needed for human survival in different environments.
  • Mission Simulator: Illustrates how mission duration may influence radiation exposure, bone and muscle loss, sleep and stress.
  • Scientific Library: Provides educational information about space physiology, health risks and protective measures.

What benefits does it have?

ASTERA makes complex space science and human physiology easier to understand through interactive 3D visuals, comparisons and simulations. It helps students, educators and space enthusiasts explore the challenges astronauts may face during space missions. It also highlights possible protective measures such as exercise, radiation shielding, hydration, nutrition, oxygen systems and medical monitoring.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to improve awareness of human health and survival challenges in space. ASTERA encourages people to think beyond planetary exploration and understand the importance of protecting human life during future long-duration missions to the Moon, Mars and beyond. It aims to make space science more accessible, engaging and educational.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed as a web application using:

  • HTML5 – Website structure and content.
  • CSS3 – Styling, responsive layouts and visual design.
  • JavaScript – Interactive features, simulations and calculations.
  • Three.js (WebGL) – 3D planetary visuals and the interactive human body model.
  • HTML Canvas – Visual rendering and mission data graphs.
  • External Three.js library – 3D graphics rendering.

The project is browser-based and does not require specialized hardware.

How is the project creative and innovative?

ASTERA brings planetary exploration and human physiology together in one interactive platform. Instead of presenting only text and scientific facts, it allows users to select a world, explore its environmental conditions, inspect the human body and understand possible health effects. The combination of 3D visualization, planet selection, body-system exploration, activity simulations and mission-duration estimates creates an engaging learning experience.

What factors did the team consider?

We considered scientific relevance, educational value, usability, visual clarity, accessibility and the challenges of long-duration human spaceflight. We also considered environmental differences between planets, astronaut health risks, available survival technologies and the importance of clearly communicating uncertainty.

The simulator uses simplified models and educational estimates. Established findings, approximate references, illustrative values and unknowns are labelled so users can distinguish documented information from projections. It is an educational tool, not a medical device or a source of actual astronaut measurements.

Our vision: To help humanity understand the challenges of living beyond Earth and prepare for a safer future in space.
